sources.quote: Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation (CASL) has been in force since 2014
sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
sources.title: Canada's anti-spam legislation
sources.evidence: The majority of CASL's provisions entered into force on July 1, 2014. Under CASL, individuals and businesses are required to obtain consent from customers before sending them commercial electronic messages, such as emails or texts.

sources.quote: The statutory maximum is CAD $1 million per violation for an individual and $10 million for a business
sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation | CRTC
sources.evidence: The maximum amount of an administrative monetary penalty (AMP) per violation for an individual is $1 million, and for a business it is $10 million. CASL applies so long as the commercial electronic message (CEM) is sent using a computer system located in Canada (s.12(1) of CASL), and CEMs sent to recipients in Canada from another country must comply with CASL.

sources.quote: The law also covers installing software and altering transmission data
sources.title: Compliance and Enforcement Information Bulletin CRTC 2012-549 | CRTC
sources.evidence: The Commission considers that a default toggling state that assumes consent cannot be used as a means of obtaining express consent for sending commercial electronic messages, altering transmission data in electronic messages, or installing a computer program on another person's computer in the course of a commercial activity. Express consent can be obtained through opt-in consent mechanisms and cannot be obtained through opt-out consent mechanisms.

sources.title: Compliance and Enforcement Information Bulletin CRTC 2012-549 PDF version
sources.evidence: A default toggling state that assumes consent cannot be used as a means of obtaining express consent under the Act. Express consent must be obtained through an opt-in mechanism, where the end user must take a positive action to indicate their consent, such as providing a blank box which a user can check off. A request for consent must contain a statement indicating that the person whose consent is sought can withdraw their consent.

sources.publisher: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
sources.title: Getting consent to send email
sources.evidence: Implied consent may be valid for up to 2 years—or just 6 months in the case of inquiries or applications. For example, as a business, you may have implied consent from someone who has purchased something or submitted an inquiry. Every unsubscribe request must be actioned within 10 business days or less and at no cost to the recipient.

sources.quote: the person published their business email address without a statement saying they do not want unsolicited messages, and your message relates to their role
sources.title: From Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation (CASL) Guidance on Implied Consent | CRTC
sources.evidence: Consent is implied if: the person to whom the message is sent has conspicuously published the electronic address to which the message is sent; the publication is not accompanied by a statement that the person does not wish to receive unsolicited CEMs at the electronic address; and the message is relevant to the person's business, role, functions or duties in a business or official capacity. The conspicuous publication exemption does not provide a broad licence to contact any electronic address found online.

sources.quote: That contact information must stay valid for 60 days after the message
sources.title: Information to be included in a commercial electronic message (CASL infographic)
sources.evidence: You must include your mailing address, and one of: a phone number to access an agent or a voice messaging system, an email address, or a web address for you or the person on whose behalf you are sending the message. These contact methods must be accurate and valid for a minimum of 60 days after sending the message.

sources.quote: Every CEM must include a clearly visible, no-cost unsubscribe mechanism
sources.title: Compliance and Enforcement Information Bulletin CRTC 2012-548 | CRTC
sources.evidence: Unsubscribe mechanisms must be usable at no cost, and a consumer must be able to make unsubscribe requests either to a specified electronic address, or through a link accessible via a web browser. An unsubscribe mechanism must be readily performed: accessed without difficulty or delay, simple, quick and easy for the consumer. Effect must be given to unsubscribe requests without delay, no later than 10 business days after the request is sent.

sources.quote: If someone fills out your contact form or requests a quote, answering that request is not a CEM requiring separate consent
sources.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation | CRTC
sources.evidence: If you are sending a CEM that is a response to a request, inquiry or complaint, requested by the person to whom the message is sent, you do not need to comply with section 6 of CASL. Therefore you do not need consent or to meet the information requirements and add an unsubscribe mechanism to the CEM. The prohibition in section 6 also does not apply to CEMs sent by an individual who has a personal or family relationship with the recipient.

sources.quote: a single message to someone referred by a person who has a relationship with both of you, naming the referrer
sources.title: Information Session on Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation | CRTC
sources.evidence: There is an exception to the consent requirement for the first commercial electronic message sent following a referral if the referral is made by an individual who has an existing business relationship, an existing non-business relationship, a family relationship or a personal relationship with the sender and any of those relationships with the recipient of the CEM. The full name of the individual who made the referral and a statement that the CEM is sent as a result of a referral must be in the CEM. Only one CEM may be sent without obtaining the consent of the recipient.

flags.quote: for at least three years after the relationship ends
flags.issue: CASL sets no prescribed retention period for consent records. The CRTC states there is no period in the legislation setting out how long records should be kept and that senders should retain records demonstrating consent for as long as they will be contacting the person, so presenting three years after the relationship ends as the rule is not what the regulator says.
